subject: Critical Thinking
title: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc: After Therefore Because?
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc: After Therefore Because?.

hook.text: 'I wore my lucky socks and we won the game.' Your socks didn't cause the victory. Sequence isn't causation.

buildup.text: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: 'after this, therefore because of this.' Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B.

discovery.text: It's the basis of most superstitions. A rooster crows before dawn — but the rooster doesn't cause the sunrise.

twist.text: Medical quackery exploits this ruthlessly. Take a remedy, then improve naturally. You credit the remedy.

climax.text: To prove causation over temporal sequence, you need repeated trials, control groups, and mechanism.

punchline.text: What came first isn't necessarily what caused it.

quiz.question: What does 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' mean?
options: After this, therefore because of this — falsely assuming sequence equals causation

details.summary: Post hoc ergo propter hoc assumes that because one event followed another, the first caused the second. A rooster crows before sunrise, so the rooster must cause the sunrise. Sequence does not prove causation.
details.whyItMatters: This fallacy creates superstitions, medical myths, and policy errors whenever people assume temporal sequence equals causal connection.
takeaways: Temporal sequence alone does not establish causation
Coincidences are far more common than we intuitively expect
The fallacy drives superstition and pseudomedical beliefs

faq.question: How does the post hoc fallacy contribute to medical pseudoscience?
faq.answer: If symptoms improve after taking a remedy, people assume the remedy caused the improvement. But many conditions improve naturally, and regression to the mean is common. Without a controlled comparison, the causal claim is unfounded.

faq.question: What distinguishes the post hoc fallacy from legitimate causal inference?
faq.answer: Legitimate causal inference requires temporal precedence plus a plausible mechanism, elimination of alternative explanations, and ideally experimental or statistical control. Temporal sequence is necessary but never sufficient by itself.
